problem:
Kaveri Textiles exports fabric from India to buyers in Europe, and its finance director has a simple complaint: the money leaves the buyer quickly and arrives in India slowly, and nobody can say who owns each part of the journey. The European buyer pays in euros, the Indian exporter needs rupees, the payment crosses a domestic euro rail, a cross-border bridge, an FX conversion and a domestic Indian rail, and each participant reports only its own leg. When a payment is late, the exporter calls the buyer, the buyer calls its bank, and the bank calls the bridge operator, and the answer is always that the other party holds the money.

The operating model has to name every participant and give each one a single responsibility. The originating bank owns the euro leg and the customer instruction. The bridge operator owns the orchestration, the FX execution and the end-to-end state. The Indian partner bank owns the INR leg and the credit to the exporter. Compliance screening, liquidity and settlement are owned explicitly, not shared vaguely, so a failure has one owner and one escalation path.

The model must also be honest about timing. A domestic euro leg can complete inside the 10-second SCT Inst window, and a domestic Indian leg can complete instantly on UPI or IMPS, but the end-to-end payment is only complete when every leg confirms. The customer promise must reflect that, not the speed of the fastest leg.
solution:
Define the operating model as a table of participants, responsibilities and handoffs. The originating bank validates the instruction, runs Verification of Payee on the euro leg, screens the payment, and releases the euro leg as SCT Inst or as a One-Leg-Out Instant Credit Transfer where one leg sits outside SEPA. The bridge operator receives the euro confirmation, revalidates the FX quote, checks settlement liquidity, and instructs the INR leg. The Indian partner bank executes the INR leg on the rail that fits the amount and urgency, UPI for small instant transfers within its limits, IMPS for instant bank transfers typically capped by banks around Rs 5 lakh, NEFT in half-hourly batches, or RTGS for individual real-time settlement from Rs 2 lakh, and confirms the credit.

Compliance is split by ownership: the originating bank owns sanctions, AML and fraud screening on the euro side, the bridge operator owns corridor-level screening and sanctions list currency, and the Indian partner bank owns local regulatory checks on the INR leg. No participant may bypass a mandatory check to protect a speed target, and each check has a synchronous decision deadline and a fail-closed rule.

Settlement and liquidity are owned by the bridge operator, which holds the corridor settlement accounts, funds them to the agreed level, and reconciles them daily. FX risk sits with the party named in the quote contract, and the quote expiry is enforced at execution. The end-to-end state is owned by the bridge operator and is the only status shown to the customer as the corridor status; leg statuses are shown as supporting detail, never as the headline. A failure after sender debit follows a defined path: establish whether the debit is provisional, final or held, await or request the missing confirmation, and only then return funds or compensate, with exactly one financial effect.

decision.question: A EUR 25,000 payment from a European buyer to Kaveri Textiles has been debited from the buyer, the euro leg is confirmed, but the INR leg has produced no confirmation after the corridor timeout. The learner must decide who owns the next action and what the customer should be told.

options.label: A
options.detail: Credit the exporter from the bridge suspense account so the exporter is not kept waiting.

options.label: B
options.detail: Place the payment in the bridge investigation state, owned by the bridge operator, tell both customers the INR leg is unconfirmed, and resolve it through leg reconciliation before any retry or compensation.

options.label: C
options.detail: Tell the exporter the payment is complete because the buyer was debited.

options.label: D
options.detail: Ask the buyer to send the payment again immediately.

decisionRationale: Option B is correct because the bridge operator owns the end-to-end state, an unconfirmed leg is an investigation case, and no retry or compensation happens before the leg states are established. Option C is wrong because a sender debit does not prove beneficiary credit. Option D is wrong because a blind resend risks a duplicate payment. Option A is wrong because crediting from suspense before the leg outcome is known creates a double-payment risk.

steps.title: Instructs a EUR payment to Kaveri Textiles with invoice reference and purpose.
Validates the instruction, runs Verification of Payee and screening, and obtains an FX quote.
Accepts the FX quote and confirms the payment.
Releases the euro leg and confirms it through the instant clearing mechanism.
Receives the euro confirmation, revalidates the FX quote and checks settlement liquidity.
Executes the FX conversion at the agreed rate and instructs the INR leg to the Indian partner bank.
Runs local compliance checks and executes the INR leg on the selected domestic rail.
Credits Kaveri Textiles and returns the confirmation with the credit timestamp.
Matches all leg confirmations, marks the corridor payment Complete, and publishes one customer timeline.

happy: The buyer accepts the FX quote, screening clears, and the euro leg confirms inside the SCT Inst 10-second window. The bridge operator revalidates the quote while it is still valid, executes the conversion, and instructs the INR leg. The Indian partner bank runs its local checks and credits Kaveri Textiles on the selected domestic rail. The bridge operator matches the euro confirmation, the FX execution and the INR credit, marks the payment Complete, and both customers see a single timeline with the applied rate, the fees and the confirmation time for each leg.

negative.title: Asynchronous legs with no destination confirmation
negative.detail: The euro leg is accepted but the destination system has not confirmed beneficiary credit. Model each leg separately with an overall orchestration state, apply the scheme timeout, enter an investigation state when the threshold is reached, and do not blindly resubmit.

negative.title: Payment fails after sender debit
negative.detail: The sender is debited but the receiving system reports a technical failure or no final response. Establish whether the debit is provisional, final or held, use scheme rules and leg status to decide whether to await confirmation, return funds or investigate, and ensure exactly one financial effect.

negative.title: Compliance screening threatens the instant SLA
negative.detail: A mandatory check cannot complete inside the rail processing window. Apply the approved fail-closed rule, hold or reject under the documented procedure, escalate within the screening SLA, and never bypass screening for speed.

negative.title: Duplicate callback or late success
negative.detail: A late success arrives after a timeout, or a confirmation callback is delivered twice. Resolve the transaction from durable leg state and unique financial event IDs, so a late success and a refund cannot both take effect, and a duplicate callback cannot double-post.

technical: Give every corridor payment a single orchestration ID plus a leg ID for each leg, and propagate the instruction ID, end-to-end ID and UETR where applicable unchanged across all legs. Keep a durable leg-level state machine for the euro leg, the bridge settlement leg and the INR leg, with an overall orchestration state that only moves to Complete on the required confirmations. Make every financial posting idempotent on its financial event ID, and store FX quote, consent, screening decision and leg confirmation as separate audit events with source and timestamp. Translate data through a canonical model that preserves the structured or hybrid address, the purpose code and the rail-specific references, and never fabricate a value missing from the source message. Define the corridor timeout, the investigation trigger and the compensation rules in configuration, and test the race between a late success and a return so exactly one outcome is possible.

accounting: Each leg posts its own linked entries: the euro receipt credits a corridor settlement account, the FX execution posts the conversion at the agreed rate with the spread recorded separately, and the INR leg debits the settlement account and credits the exporter. A leg that confirms without its counterpart is parked in a corridor suspense worklist with the bridge operator as owner and a defined SLA, and no compensation is posted until the leg states are established. Nostro and settlement account reconciliation runs daily on the bridge accounts with same-day break ageing, and fees are posted per leg so the customer can see the cost of each stage. Operations works four queues: unconfirmed legs past timeout, screening holds, quote expiries and unmatched settlements, each with its own escalation time and a rule that no item is retried without a fresh decision.

scenarios.given: the originating leg is accepted but destination confirmation is absent
scenarios.then: the payment enters an unknown or investigation state. it is not blindly resubmitted

scenarios.given: a timeout followed by a late success
scenarios.then: the system resolves the transaction without both crediting the beneficiary and refunding the sender. exactly one financial effect is recorded

questions.question: Who owns the end-to-end state of a corridor payment?
options: The bridge operator, as the orchestrator
questions.explanation: The bridge operator owns orchestration and the end-to-end state. Each participant owns its own leg.

questions.question: Which Indian rail settles individually in real time with a minimum of Rs 2 lakh?
questions.explanation: RTGS settles individually in real time, minimum Rs 2 lakh, with no RBI maximum.

questions.question: A sender is debited but the destination reports no final response. What must the bank establish first?
options: Whether the debit is provisional, final or held
questions.explanation: The debit character determines whether to await confirmation, return funds or investigate, and it protects exactly-once financial effect.

questions.question: How is NEFT settlement organised?
questions.explanation: NEFT settles in half-hourly batches and operates 24x7x365, as do RTGS and IMPS.
